Last summer, my dad's small landscaping business in Fresno almost went under because he was still using paper invoices and a shoebox full of receipts. I watched him spend three hours every Sunday trying to figure out which clients owed money. That's when I decided to build him a billing system.

I'd never coded before. I spent six weeks teaching myself Python and SQL through YouTube videos and Stack Overflow, staying up until midnight most nights. By August, I had a working app that let him track invoices, send reminders, and see his cash flow in real time. When my dad used it for the first time, he actually cried. He told me he could finally take a Saturday off.

That project changed everything for me. I realized that technology isn't just for Silicon Valley—it's a tool to solve real problems for people like my parents who built their lives here without fancy resources. My dad's business isn't unique. There are thousands of small business owners in the Central Valley struggling with the same thing.

I want to study computer science and come back to Fresno to build tech solutions specifically for local businesses that can't afford expensive software. I'm not trying to move away and make it big somewhere else. I want to fix what I see broken in my own community.

When I'm researching universities, I'm specifically looking for programs with strong connections to local entrepreneurship and small business support. I want professors and classmates who understand that engineering isn't just about innovation for its own sake—it's about serving people. Your school's partnership with the Central Valley Small Business Development Center caught my attention because it shows you actually care about our region, not just Silicon Valley.

That summer taught me that motivation isn't something you find—it's something you build when you see someone you love struggling and realize you have the power to help.

Junior year, I realized our school's robotics club was basically dead. We had maybe four people showing up, and nobody had competed since 2019. I pitched to Mr. Chen, the faculty advisor, that we could actually build something for the state competition in March. He was skeptical but gave me a shot.

I spent two weeks recruiting. I went to the engineering classes, talked to kids in the hallway, posted on the school Discord. By February, we had twelve people. Most had never built a robot before. I divided us into teams: mechanical, electrical, programming. I'm decent at coding, so I led the programming side with Marcus and Priya.

The problem was our budget. We had maybe $400. I spent hours researching cheaper suppliers and found used parts on eBay. We salvaged a motor from an old drill. It was honestly kind of ridiculous, but it worked. By competition day in early March, we'd built this clunky thing that could pick up game pieces and score points.

We didn't place. We came in eighth out of sixteen. Our robot failed halfway through one match because the wiring was loose. I was genuinely disappointed, but then something unexpected happened. During the awards ceremony, three freshmen came up to me asking when we'd start building for next year.

What I learned wasn't about winning. It was that people actually want to be part of something if someone gives them the chance. I'd been waiting for a club to magically exist instead of just starting it myself. Also, I learned that leadership isn't about having all the answers. When Marcus suggested we try a different wheel configuration and I listened instead of insisting on my design, that's when things actually improved.

We're already meeting this summer for next year. We have eighteen people registered now.

Last summer, I was working at Target in the electronics section when I noticed an older woman struggling to find a phone. She kept asking employees questions, but they'd give quick answers and move on. She looked completely lost, so I spent twenty minutes with her, explaining the difference between Android and iPhone, showing her how to check if a phone worked with her carrier, and answering the same question three times when she forgot what I'd said.

When she finally bought a phone, she thanked me and told me her grandson had moved to Colorado and she wanted to FaceTime with him. That hit different. I realized most of my coworkers saw her as a transaction, but she was actually trying to connect with her family across the country.

After that, I started noticing other customers who seemed confused or frustrated. I'd check in with them even when they didn't ask, walked people through processes, and sometimes just listened to their stories about why they needed something. My manager noticed and asked me to train new hires on customer service, which I did for the rest of summer.

What stuck with me is how small actions create real impact. That woman probably could have figured things out eventually or asked someone else, but she would have felt rushed and dumb. Instead, she felt helped. It made me realize that prosocial stuff isn't always about massive volunteer projects or changing systems. Sometimes it's just about being present when someone needs it.

I'm thinking about how this applies to whatever field I end up in, whether that's engineering or policy work. I want to build or create things that actually consider the people using them, not just the technical specs. That summer taught me that understanding people matters as much as understanding problems.

My junior year, I started rebuilding a 1987 Honda Civic with my dad in our garage. Not for a school project or to impress anyone—just because I wanted to understand how it actually worked.

Every Saturday for eight months, I'd spend four or five hours under that car. My hands got permanently stained with grease. I'd watch YouTube videos at night, pausing constantly, rewinding, trying to understand why the timing belt mattered or how the carburetor actually fed fuel. When I'd mess up and have to redo the valve adjustment three times, I'd feel genuinely frustrated, but I'd keep going back the next weekend.

What surprised me was how much I didn't care about finishing it. We still haven't driven it anywhere. The engine runs now, but the interior's a disaster and the brakes need work. My friends thought I was insane—they'd be out doing stuff on Saturdays, and I'm choosing to be covered in grease in a hot garage.

But I realized I was doing it because that moment when I finally understood something—like when I got the timing right and the engine actually fired up smoothly—was genuinely satisfying in a way grades or awards never were. It wasn't about having a finished car to show off. It was about the problem-solving itself, the learning process, the figuring things out.

That experience changed how I think about what I want to study. I'm drawn to engineering and technology, but specifically the kind where I'm constantly solving problems and learning systems deeply, not just completing assignments. That car taught me I'm someone who gets motivated by understanding how things work, not by external rewards or deadlines. It's made me pickier about what I commit my time to, because I know what real intrinsic motivation feels like now.

Last spring, I noticed our school's recycling program was basically broken. Bins were mixed up, contamination was everywhere, and most people just threw stuff in the trash anyway. I got frustrated watching it fail, so in March I actually did something about it.

I pitched the idea to Mr. Chen, our environmental science teacher, and he let me run with it. I recruited four juniors—Marcus, Priya, Devon, and Sophie—who were in my lunch period. We started by auditing what was happening. I spent two weeks tracking what went into each bin across the cafeteria and classrooms. The data was bad: we were contaminating about 40 percent of recyclables.

We created a simple system. I designed color-coded labels and made a one-page guide showing exactly what goes where, with pictures so it was actually clear. We printed 200 copies and put them everywhere. Then we split up: Marcus and Devon managed cafeteria bins during lunch, Priya and Sophie did classrooms, and I tracked weekly numbers and adjusted things.

By May, contamination dropped to 12 percent. We collected 2,800 pounds that semester, up from around 1,600 the previous spring. The district actually noticed and asked if we'd present to other schools.

What I learned wasn't just about recycling logistics. It was that people aren't lazy—they just need clarity and someone to actually care enough to make it easy. Marcus told me later he stayed involved because I showed up every single day, didn't just talk about it. That stuck with me. Real leadership isn't about being the smartest person in the room. It's about seeing something broken, getting other people to believe it matters, and doing the unglamorous work of following through. I want to study engineering partly because I want to solve bigger problems this same way.

Last summer, our neighborhood's community center was about to close the free tech program because nobody wanted to teach it. I'd been volunteering there since sophomore year, and I knew maybe twenty kids depended on those Tuesday and Thursday sessions. So in June, I talked to the director, Marcus, and basically said I'd run it myself.

I'd never taught anything before. I started by asking each kid what they actually wanted to learn instead of assuming. Turns out most of them cared about making apps, not just coding basics. I spent two weeks redesigning the curriculum and reached out to my cousin Derek, who works in software development, to help me understand what would actually be useful. He came in twice a month to do workshops.

By August, we had grown from twelve regular attendees to thirty-one. I had to split into two groups and recruit another volunteer, this girl named Priya from the high school who was really into Python. We started tracking projects—by the end of summer, eight kids had built simple games or apps they could show their families. One kid, Carlos, made a calculator app and was genuinely proud of it.

The hardest part wasn't organizing the sessions. It was dealing with kids who showed up once and quit, or handling the time when Derek canceled and I had to improvise an entire lesson on databases. I learned I'm not naturally patient, but I could be more patient if I actually cared about the outcome, which I did.

When I presented the program results to Marcus in September, he asked if I'd continue as lead instructor this year. I said yes. I realized that leadership isn't about being the smartest person or having everything figured out. It's about noticing something broken and being stubborn enough to try fixing it, even when you're not sure you can.

When I was fifteen, I decided I wanted to build a robot for the First Robotics competition. The problem was I'd never coded before, had no engineering experience, and our school didn't have a team. I gave myself eight months to start one from scratch before the competition deadline in March.

I spent the first month teaching myself Python through YouTube and online courses, spending maybe three hours every night after school. I realized I needed to recruit people, so I posted flyers around school and held an informational meeting in February. Only six people showed up, but that was enough. We divided into two groups—mechanical and programming—and I led the programming side.

The biggest obstacle came in December when we discovered our code had fundamental errors that would take weeks to fix. We'd wasted almost a month on the wrong approach. I nearly quit, but I called the mentors at a local tech company I'd emailed months earlier. Three of them agreed to volunteer with us weekly, and suddenly we had actual engineers reviewing our work.

We met every single day from January through March, sometimes until 8 PM on school nights. The night before competition, we were still debugging. We didn't win first place—we placed fourth in our regional—but our robot actually worked. We scored points. Kids who'd never programmed anything had written functioning code.

What stuck with me wasn't the placement. It was realizing that goals don't happen because you're smart or talented. They happen because you stay committed when things get hard, and because you're willing to ask for help. I learned that failing at something is just information, not a reflection of your capability. Now when I face something difficult in school or projects, I remember that feeling of pushing through December when everything felt broken. That's when I know I'm actually learning something real.

Last spring, my robotics team at Lincoln High was building a competition bot for the state championship. We had Marcus on mechanical design, Priya handling the coding, Devon managing logistics, and me coordinating between departments. Three weeks before competition, Marcus and Priya completely disagreed on the arm mechanism. Marcus wanted a heavier, more durable design. Priya insisted it would slow our processing speed too much. They stopped talking to each other, just left passive-aggressive notes on our shared document.

I realized our timeline was collapsing. Instead of picking sides, I scheduled a two-hour session where we actually listened. Marcus explained the arm had failed during practice runs. Priya showed her speed calculations proving the added weight would cost us points in the timed challenges. Then I suggested something neither had considered separately—reinforcing specific joints with carbon fiber instead of overbuilding the whole arm. It was lighter than Marcus's version and faster than Priya's worst-case scenario.

We tested the hybrid design for two days. It worked. Better than either original idea.

What struck me wasn't just that we fixed the problem. It was realizing how much I'd been trying to be the person who had all the answers. I thought my job was preventing conflict, but actually my job was creating space for it. Marcus and Priya both knew things I didn't. The solution only existed because we stopped pretending we could figure it out alone.

We placed second at states. The arm mechanism held up through every round. But honestly, the design itself mattered less to me than understanding that good teamwork isn't about harmony—it's about making sure everyone's expertise actually gets heard and combined. That changed how I approach problems now, especially knowing I want to work in engineering.

Last spring, my robotics team was building a competition bot for the state finals, and we were stuck. Marcus, our lead programmer, had written code that kept crashing during test runs. Sarah, who designed the mechanical arm, insisted the problem was structural. I was handling logistics and team coordination, and honestly, they weren't listening to each other anymore.

We had four weeks left, and the tension was killing our progress. I called a meeting and suggested we actually trace through one failed run together, line by line. Marcus walked us through his code while Sarah watched the robot's movements on video. That's when Sarah noticed the arm jerked right before the crash—not because of her design, but because Marcus's loop was updating position data every five milliseconds instead of fifty. They'd been arguing about different problems.

Marcus rewrote the timing protocol while Sarah reinforced two joints that were experiencing unexpected stress from the corrected movements. I documented everything we learned and created a testing checklist so we'd catch similar issues faster.

The bot qualified for finals, and we placed third in the state. But here's what actually stuck with me: we didn't win because we were individually smarter. We won because Marcus realized his code needed context from mechanical reality, Sarah understood software constraints shaped her design options, and I learned that my job wasn't just scheduling—it was making space for people to actually hear each other.

Before this, I thought teamwork meant everyone doing their part and hoping it fits together. Now I know it's messier. It's stopping to translate between people who speak different technical languages. It's defending someone's idea even when you're frustrated with them. That's the version of teamwork I'm bringing to whatever engineering or tech problem I tackle next.

Last summer, I noticed my neighbor Mrs. Chen couldn't afford insulin. She'd been rationing it, skipping doses to make her supply last until her next disability check. I'd see her sitting on her porch in the afternoons, and one day she mentioned missing her granddaughter's birthday party because the clinic visit cost too much.

I started researching and realized the problem wasn't just Mrs. Chen's situation. In our county, nearly 40% of seniors on fixed incomes skip medications due to cost. Pharmaceutical companies price insulin at $300 a vial while other countries pay $30. It's a broken system where profit matters more than survival.

I couldn't fix that alone, but I could do something. I contacted the Meals on Wheels coordinator at our community center and proposed adding a medication assistance component. With their help, I learned which programs actually worked—GoodRx, patient assistance programs, generic alternatives—things Mrs. Chen didn't know existed.

Over three months, I helped twelve neighbors navigate these resources. Most qualified for programs cutting their costs 60-80%. I created a simple one-page guide in English and Mandarin since our area has a large Chinese immigrant population facing the same barriers. The community center printed 200 copies and distributed them through their network.

Mrs. Chen now pays $35 monthly for her insulin through a manufacturer program I found. She brought me dumplings and cried.

What I learned wasn't about feeling good. It was that problems aren't usually about individual failure—they're structural. Mrs. Chen isn't poor because she's irresponsible; the system is designed so people like her get squeezed. Real help means understanding why something's broken and connecting people to actual solutions, not just sympathy. I'm considering public policy because this experience showed me how systems either trap people or set them free.

Last summer, I spent three months building a weather station from scratch in my backyard. Not for a class project or competition—my physics teacher didn't even know about it until months later. I started because I was frustrated watching my tomato plants fail, and I wanted to understand the actual humidity and temperature patterns in my yard, not just check some generic forecast.

I taught myself Arduino programming through YouTube tutorials and bought a $40 microcontroller kit. The first two weeks were terrible. My humidity sensor kept giving me readings of 200%, which made no sense. I'd spend entire afternoons debugging code, rewriting loops, checking connections with a multimeter my dad lent me. My friends were at the pool, and I was in my garage sweating over a circuit board.

But then something clicked. I redesigned the sensor calibration, got accurate readings, and added a small LCD screen that displayed real-time data. By week four, I had wind speed, rainfall, and barometric pressure sensors working together. I mounted everything on a pole and started logging data every fifteen minutes.

What kept me going wasn't any external motivation. There were no grades, no college resume points I was thinking about. I just wanted to see if I could do it, and once I started, I was genuinely curious about what the data would show. I learned that my backyard gets completely different wind patterns depending on which direction the storm comes from. My tomatoes actually did better after I adjusted watering based on real humidity data, not guessing.

The real lesson wasn't technical, though. I discovered that I actually enjoy the problem-solving process itself—the frustration, the small victories, the obsessive tinkering. It made me realize I want to study engineering not because it's practical, but because I like building things to understand how systems work.

Last summer, I noticed our apartment complex in East Memphis had zero water fountains in the common areas, and most residents were elderly or low-income families. I'd see kids drinking from garden hoses and people buying bottled water they couldn't afford. It seemed like a simple problem, but it pointed to something bigger—how infrastructure gets ignored in neighborhoods like ours.

I started researching and learned that our city's budget allocations heavily favored wealthier districts. I spent three weeks documenting everything: taking photos, interviewing residents like Mrs. Chen who lives in 204 and spent forty dollars a week on water bottles, and mapping out where fountains should go based on foot traffic.

Then I actually did something about it instead of just complaining. I contacted our city councilman's office with a specific proposal: install two refillable water stations using existing electrical lines near the playground and community center. I included my cost breakdown, maintenance plan, and a petition with signatures from forty-seven residents.

The councilman's assistant met with me in person. She said they'd been getting generic complaints forever, but never actual solutions. They took my proposal to the city planning committee. Six months later, they installed one fountain, and they're planning a second.

What I learned wasn't that I'm some hero—I'm not. I learned that problems don't get fixed because nobody knows exactly what to fix or who to ask. It's easy to feel helpless about systems, but sometimes they're just waiting for someone to show up with specific information and say, "Here's what we need." I want to study public policy because I realized how much power is sitting there unused, waiting for people who actually understand their communities to step in and use it.

Last summer, I noticed my neighbor Mrs. Chen, who's 78, struggling to carry groceries up the three flights to her apartment in our building in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. She'd make multiple trips, sometimes sitting on the stairs catching her breath. I learned her kids lived in California and visited maybe twice a year. Then her daughter mentioned the building's elevator had been broken for four months.

I started asking around. Turns out the landlord, who owns twelve buildings in the neighborhood, wasn't fixing it because the court case with the previous tenant was still pending. Mrs. Chen wasn't the only one suffering—a guy on the second floor had stopped going to his dialysis appointments because the stairs exhausted him.

Instead of just helping Mrs. Chen individually, I started documenting everything. I took photos of the broken elevator, got statements from five other tenants about how it affected them, and found the housing violation code. I discovered the city had a tenant hotline I'd never heard of. With help from my mom, I filed a complaint and contacted the local council member's office.

It took two months, but the pressure worked. The landlord finally fixed it in October. Mrs. Chen actually cried when it reopened.

What stuck with me wasn't just solving one person's problem. It was realizing how many people were suffering from the same issue but didn't know who to contact or how to push back. The landlord was counting on that—on people being isolated and not knowing their rights. I learned that systemic problems need systemic solutions, not just individual kindness. That's why I'm interested in public policy. I want to understand how these systems work so I can help fix them at a larger scale.

Last summer, I noticed that the senior center on Maple Street in my town was struggling. Mrs. Chen, who runs the place, mentioned they couldn't afford updated computers, so residents couldn't video call their grandkids or access telehealth appointments. Most of them are on fixed incomes and can't afford home internet.

I realized this wasn't just about old equipment. Rural areas like ours get overlooked by tech companies, and seniors get forgotten in the digital divide conversation. So I started small. I talked to the IT teacher at my school, Mr. Rodriguez, and we got a grant from the library foundation for five refurbished laptops. But I knew that wasn't enough.

I organized a monthly tech clinic where I teach basics every second Saturday. Started with five people showing up. Now it's usually fifteen to twenty. I created simple printed guides with large fonts for Gmail and Zoom because I learned quickly that YouTube tutorials move too fast for them. My neighbor Tom, who's seventy-two, finally got to see his daughter's newborn in California. He cried.

The bigger thing I learned was that the problem wasn't really the technology. It was that nobody had asked what they needed. I assumed they wanted to learn, but really they wanted connection. When Mrs. Chen's daughter helped translate for Mr. Lopez, who speaks mainly Spanish, everything changed. He started coming regularly.

I'm planning to expand this to other senior centers in the county, but I'm also realizing I need to understand policy better. Why don't internet providers invest in rural areas? How do funding decisions get made? That's why I'm interested in studying public policy or social technology. This experience showed me that fixing real problems requires understanding systems, not just good intentions.

Last summer, my mom's restaurant in Des Moines almost closed. She couldn't track inventory, payroll was a nightmare, and customers complained about wait times. I watched her stress at the kitchen table with spreadsheets and receipts everywhere, and I realized the problem wasn't her work ethic—it was the systems.

I taught myself Python over three weeks using YouTube and Stack Overflow. By week four, I'd built a basic inventory management system that tracked stock levels and flagged items running low. It wasn't perfect, but it cut her ordering time in half. Then I added a simple scheduling app so she could manage staff shifts without manual spreadsheets. She cried when I showed her.

What actually motivated me wasn't some abstract goal—it was seeing her skip lunch because she was too overwhelmed. It was concrete. It was my mom.

That experience showed me small business owners across Iowa face the same problem. They're skilled at what they do, but they lack affordable tech solutions. Most software is built for corporations, not a twenty-person restaurant or a local manufacturing shop.

I want to study computer science at Iowa State because I want to build technology specifically for small businesses in the Midwest. Your program's partnership with the Iowa Small Business Development Center is exactly what I need. I've already talked to the center's director, and they're interested in having me work on real projects while I'm a student.

I'm not interested in moving to Silicon Valley. I want to come back to Des Moines. My mom's business is still here. Hundreds of others like hers are here. That's where I can actually make a difference, not in theory, but in someone's real life.

Last summer, I decided I wanted to learn coding because I kept feeling left out when my older cousin Marcus talked about his internship at a tech company. I told myself I'd be fluent in Python by September, which honestly sounds ridiculous now.

I found a free course on Codecademy and started in June. The first two weeks went fine—basic syntax, simple loops, nothing too hard. But then I hit functions and got completely stuck. I'd spend an hour staring at my screen, watching error messages pop up, and just close the laptop. My mom kept asking if I was still doing my coding thing, and I'd lie and say yeah.

By mid-July, I'd basically quit. I was embarrassed because I'd told like five people about my goal, including my dad, and I felt stupid for giving up. But then my friend Jasmine, who's going into engineering, asked why I stopped. Instead of making an excuse, I actually told her I didn't understand functions. She sat down with me for maybe thirty minutes and walked through an actual project she was building—a calculator for splitting restaurant bills. Seeing it applied to something real clicked for me.

After that, I changed my approach. I stopped trying to rush through lessons and started building small things—a temperature converter, a grade calculator for my classes. By late August, I'd built a basic app that tracked how many hours I spent on different activities. It wasn't perfect, but it worked.

I didn't become fluent in Python like I'd promised myself. But I learned that having a goal and actually pursuing it are completely different things. The real progress happened when I stopped trying to impress people and just focused on understanding one thing at a time. That's probably more useful than the coding anyway.

Last summer, I decided I wanted to learn video editing so I could make a short documentary about my neighborhood's community garden. I'd never touched editing software before, but I kept thinking about how cool it would be to show people what happens there.

I downloaded DaVinci Resolve in June and started watching YouTube tutorials. The first week was rough. I didn't understand timelines or color grading or any of it. I'd spend two hours trying to figure out why my clips wouldn't sync properly, then give up frustrated. My friend Marcus kept telling me to just use iMovie instead, but I was stubborn about learning the real thing.

By mid-July, something clicked. I stopped watching random tutorials and actually followed one creator's entire beginner series. I started filming at the garden on Saturday mornings with my phone, just capturing people planting tomatoes and kids running around. I interviewed Mrs. Chen, who's been managing the garden for eight years, and got her talking about why it mattered to the neighborhood.

I finished the video in August. It's twelve minutes long, kind of rough in places, but it's actually watchable. My parents cried watching it. I posted it on YouTube and got like two hundred views, mostly from people at the community center.

What surprised me was how much the frustration part mattered. I realized I wasn't mad at the software being hard—I was mad that I couldn't see the thing in my head yet. Once I understood that, I could actually focus on learning instead of just wanting the result immediately.

I'm thinking about studying media production now, or maybe something with public policy where I could tell stories about communities. Either way, I learned that sticking with something uncomfortable actually teaches you something about what you're capable of.

When I was a junior, I ran for class representative basically because my friend Marcus kept saying someone needed to actually do something about lunch. I won, which surprised me because I'd never done student government before.

The first real test came when a bunch of freshmen complained that the cafeteria was cutting vegetarian options. I could've just ignored it, but I actually ate in the cafeteria every day and noticed they were right. So I set up a meeting with Mr. Chen, the food service manager, and brought a petition with about 140 signatures. I was nervous going in because I'd never negotiated anything like that before.

What helped was that I came with specific data. I'd counted the vegetarian students in each lunch period over two weeks and showed him the numbers. He told me they'd actually received complaints but didn't realize how many people cared. We worked out a compromise where they'd add one vegetarian option daily and do a full vegetarian day once a month.

The weirdest part was when students started thanking me in the halls. I realized people actually paid attention to what the class rep did. That sounds obvious now, but it made me take the job more seriously. I started attending actual budget meetings and pushing for better things instead of just announcing dances.

I learned that leadership isn't about being the loudest person or having all the answers. It's about listening to people and actually following through. Mr. Chen was willing to help once he understood the problem mattered. I also learned that doing basic things like counting data and writing things down makes you way more credible than just complaining.

It's why I'm interested in policy work. I liked that feeling of identifying a real problem and figuring out how to fix it.

I started coding at 2 AM on a Tuesday because I couldn't sleep, not because anyone assigned it. My computer science teacher, Mr. Patterson, had mentioned machine learning in passing during class, and something about it stuck with me. I downloaded Python tutorials and spent the next six months building a chatbot that could identify local news articles about water quality issues in our county.

Nobody asked me to do this. There was no assignment, no extra credit, no competition I was trying to win. I just became obsessed with the problem. My mom would find me at the kitchen table at midnight with three energy drinks, arguing with myself about whether my training data was biased. I rewrote the entire classification system twice because the first version wasn't catching articles about agricultural runoff, which bothered me more than it probably should have.

The chatbot wasn't even that good by professional standards. It missed things. But in March, I contacted the Riverside County Water Authority and showed them what I'd built. They actually used it for two months to monitor local reporting before switching to a commercial tool. That mattered to me way more than any grade could.

What I learned wasn't some profound lesson about persistence. It was simpler: I'm the kind of person who gets genuinely curious about how things work and can't let it go. I don't need external motivation to dig into something that feels important. That's not a strength I developed—it's just how my brain operates when I find the right problem. Understanding that about myself changed how I think about what I want to study. I'm not looking for prestige or a high salary. I'm looking for problems that will keep me up at 2 AM.

Junior year, my neighborhood in East Oakland had a water main break that flooded three blocks. While crews fixed pipes, I noticed something that stuck with me—families were paying bottled water prices they couldn't afford, and the city took two weeks to deliver alternatives. My mom works at Kaiser, my dad drives for Uber, and I watched them stress about the bill that month.

I decided to map the issue. I taught myself basic GIS mapping using free USGS data and created a visualization showing which Oakland neighborhoods had aging infrastructure and lowest household incomes. I spent eight weeks on it, staying after school three days a week in the computer lab, learning YouTube tutorials at night. I made mistakes constantly—coordinate systems didn't align, data was incomplete—but I kept fixing them.

By November, I'd finished something real: a map showing East Oakland had the oldest pipes and highest water costs. I presented it to our city council member at a community meeting. She actually listened. More importantly, she connected me with her policy analyst, who explained how infrastructure funding actually works. I realized the problem wasn't just broken pipes—it was that poor neighborhoods don't have the data or political power to demand maintenance budgets.

That process changed how I see problems. I learned that motivation isn't inspiration; it's showing up when the work is boring, when you don't know what you're doing, when the results feel small. I also learned I'm good at translating between technical information and what people actually need to know.

I want to study public policy with a technology focus at a school where I can keep working on infrastructure equity. Not as theory—as something that fixes my actual community. I'm applying to your program specifically because your partnership with Oakland's Planning Department means I could do real work while studying.

Last spring, I noticed our school's recycling program was basically nonexistent. We had bins, but nobody sorted anything, and I watched the custodians dump everything into the same truck. I got frustrated enough to actually do something about it.

I talked to Mr. Chen, our environmental science teacher, and he agreed to let me run a pilot program in the science wing. I recruited four friends—Marcus, Priya, and twins Jacob and Sophie—to help me design a system. We spent two weeks mapping out where bins should go, creating laminated sorting guides, and honestly, just pestering people in the hallways about why recycling mattered.

We launched in April with a competition angle. Each grade level earned points for proper sorting, and the winner got first pick of lunch seating for a week. Sounds silly, but it worked. By week three, we were sorting about 240 pounds of material weekly. By May, Mr. Chen helped us calculate that we diverted roughly 960 pounds of waste from the landfill that month alone.

The administration noticed. They asked if we could expand to the entire school for next year, which meant recruiting more students and training them. I realized I couldn't just tell people what to do—I had to make them actually care. So I made short videos with Marcus showing the landfill impact, got Priya to design a badge system people could earn, and had Sophie and Jacob lead the training sessions because they were better at explaining things than me.

What I learned wasn't about recycling. It was that leadership isn't about having the best idea—it's about recognizing what matters to other people and building a team that's genuinely invested. I couldn't have moved 960 pounds of trash alone. That's what actually stuck with me.

What hit me hardest was realizing how many problems in my neighborhood aren't unsolvable—they're just under-resourced and under-advocated for. I want to study civil engineering at Berkeley because I can see exactly what I'd do there. The program's infrastructure and sustainability focus matches what I need, and Oakland needs engineers who actually care about communities like mine, not just corporations.

I'm not going anywhere after graduation. My little sister is starting high school next year, and I want her to see someone from our block make it in engineering and come back to fix things. That's my actual plan.

Junior year, I decided to build a water filtration system for my environmental science class. Not just a basic project—I wanted it to actually work well enough to present at the state science fair in March, four months away.

I started by researching existing filters online and watching YouTube videos from engineers at water nonprofits. Then I mapped out a timeline: research by November, prototype by December, testing in January and February, final version by March. My friend Marcus helped me source materials from a hardware store in Westchester, and we spent weekends in my garage testing different combinations of sand, charcoal, and gravel.

The first prototype failed completely. Water just ran straight through without filtering anything. I realized I'd stacked the layers wrong and hadn't compressed them enough. That's when I actually called an engineer at a local water treatment facility who'd posted his email online. He spent twenty minutes explaining how pressure and particle size matter. I rebuilt the entire system based on his advice.

By January, the filter was reducing turbidity by 87 percent. I kept detailed measurements in a spreadsheet—pH levels, filtration rates, bacterial reduction. But I wasn't satisfied. I added another layer using activated coconut charcoal in February and got it to 94 percent.

I didn't win first place at the state fair—a girl from Syracuse with a better presentation won. But I placed second and got invited to demo it at a community event in May. More importantly, I learned that real progress isn't linear. Failure taught me more than early success would have. I also learned I actually enjoy the research and problem-solving part more than the final presentation part, which made me realize engineering might be the right path instead of just environmental science.

Last summer, I decided to teach myself Python because I kept hitting walls in my AP Computer Science class. Mr. Chen would explain recursion and I'd nod along, but I didn't actually get it. But then something clicked. Around week four, I built a simple program that tracked my Target shifts and calculated my weekly earnings. It was maybe thirty lines, nothing complicated, but I'd made it work without looking up the answer. I realized the problem wasn't that I was bad at coding—I just needed to build actual things instead of copying examples.

I kept going. By August, I'd written a program that scraped concert dates from websites and organized them by distance from my house. It was clunky and had bugs, but it was mine. When I got back to Mr. Chen's class in September, I understood the concepts because I'd struggled through them myself.

What I learned wasn't just about coding. I learned that motivation isn't this magical feeling that hits you. It's boring repetition and staying at your kitchen table when you want to give up. It's proving to yourself that you can figure something out, even if it takes longer than it does for other people. Now when I'm stuck, I don't assume I'm not cut out for it. I just assume I haven't spent enough time yet.

I never thought of myself as a leader until sophomore year when my physics teacher, Mr. Patterson, asked me to tutor three classmates who were struggling with circuits and energy. I was decent at physics but definitely not the smartest person in the room, so I was skeptical at first.

I started meeting with Marcus, Priya, and James every Tuesday after school in the library. The first session was rough because I just tried explaining things the way Mr. Patterson did, and they looked just as confused as before. I realized I needed to figure out why they weren't getting it, not just repeat the material faster.

With Marcus, I drew out circuits on paper and let him build them with actual wires. With Priya, I made a spreadsheet showing how voltage and current actually worked with numbers she cared about, like phone batteries. James needed me to connect everything to real-world examples, so we talked about why his gaming PC needed good power supplies.

By the end of that semester, all three passed the final exam. Marcus actually got a B minus. I was surprised how much it mattered to me that they understood, not just that they passed.

What I learned wasn't about being naturally gifted or commanding a room. It was that leadership means paying attention to how people actually think differently and adjusting yourself instead of expecting them to adjust to you. I spent more time listening to what confused them than explaining anything. It made me realize I want to study engineering or maybe policy, something where I can help other people solve problems in ways that actually work for them, not just theoretically.

Last summer, I noticed our neighborhood community center's tech lab was basically dead. Three computers from 2015, no one using it, and the director mentioned they'd lost funding for programming classes. I was frustrated because I'd learned Python there two years earlier, and it felt wrong that kids like my younger cousins wouldn't get that chance.

So I pitched an idea to Director Martinez in June: what if I ran free coding workshops using the existing equipment? She was skeptical about liability, but I worked with her to develop a plan. I created a six-week curriculum covering Python basics, spent two weeks recruiting through Instagram and flyers at the basketball court. Twenty-three kids signed up, ages nine to sixteen.

The first week was chaos. I'd prepared lesson plans, but I hadn't anticipated how differently a nine-year-old and a fifteen-year-old learn. Mira, this sixth grader, got frustrated and nearly quit. I pulled her aside, slowed down the pace for her section, and paired her with Marcus, a high school kid who was patient. By week four, Mira was helping other younger kids debug their code.

I had to adapt constantly. I created two skill tracks instead of one. I recorded sessions so kids could catch up. By week six, we'd built three simple games and a weather app. Seventeen kids completed the program. The community center director told me they're now funding an official after-school tech program based on what we proved was possible.

What I learned wasn't just about coding or teaching. I realized leadership isn't about having all the answers. It's about seeing a problem, being willing to look stupid while figuring it out, and actually listening when people need different things. Mira's success mattered more to me than the curriculum I'd planned.

Last summer, I volunteered at the Riverside Community Center in my neighborhood after noticing how many kids on my block didn't have anything to do during the day. My friend Marcus and I basically showed up one Tuesday asking if they needed help, and they immediately put us to work in their after-school program.

What struck me most wasn't that they learned programming—it was that most of them had never thought they could do it. Keisha's mom told me her daughter started talking about studying engineering, which she'd never mentioned before.

I realized I'd gone in thinking I was helping underprivileged kids or whatever, but really they taught me something. They asked questions I couldn't answer, which made me look things up and actually learn instead of coasting on what I already knew. It also showed me that I care more about explaining complicated things to people than I thought I did. I'm applying to study engineering, but I'm seriously considering a path that lets me work on education access or tech policy instead of just pure technical work.

I started coding at 2 AM on a Tuesday because I couldn't stop thinking about a problem. My friend Marcus had mentioned this app he used to track his family's grocery spending, and I thought I could build something better. No assignment, no competition, just this idea that wouldn't leave me alone.

For three months, I basically lived in my basement. I'd come home from school and immediately open my laptop. My mom thought I was losing it when she found me sketching database structures on napkins at dinner. I taught myself SQL by watching YouTube tutorials at midnight, rewinding sections five times until the logic clicked. Failed constantly. My first version crashed every time someone tried to add more than ten items. I didn't care about the failures though—I was too focused on solving the next problem.

By April, I had something functional. My family used it for two months. Not perfect, but it worked. I added features nobody asked for—recipe suggestions based on inventory, price comparisons across stores—just because I wanted to see if I could. Zero external validation. My parents didn't understand what I was building. My teachers didn't know about it.

What struck me was realizing I didn't need anyone to tell me this mattered. The work itself was the point. I wasn't chasing a grade or trying to impress someone on an application. I was just genuinely curious about whether I could create something useful from nothing.

That project taught me the difference between doing things because you think you should and doing them because you actually want to understand something. Now when I'm learning anything—whether it's JavaScript frameworks or policy analysis—I notice when I'm motivated by external stuff versus when I'm actually pulled forward by curiosity. It's made me a lot more intentional about what I commit my time to.

I spent six months trying to fix our community center's broken heating system before I actually succeeded. It started last November when Mr. Chen, who runs the after-school program I volunteer at, mentioned the boiler had stopped working. The center couldn't afford a professional repair, so I offered to figure it out.

I watched YouTube videos for two weeks and thought I had it. I replaced the thermostat, but nothing changed. I felt stupid. Then I tried bleeding the radiators like some forum said—still nothing. By January, I'd failed four different times and wasted forty dollars of my own money on parts that didn't help.

What kept me going was seeing kids in winter coats during tutoring sessions. That made quitting feel impossible, even though I wanted to.

In late February, I finally connected with Mr. Patel, a retired HVAC technician who lived nearby. He didn't just fix it—he walked me through the problem. The issue wasn't one thing. The boiler's reset button was tripped, but the water pressure was also too low. I'd been treating symptoms instead of diagnosing the actual problem.

When that heat kicked on for the first time in three months, Mr. Chen hugged me. Kids actually took off their jackets.

I learned that perseverance isn't about being stubborn or never failing. It's about staying curious when you fail. Every wrong answer taught me something about how heating systems work. If I'd quit after attempt two, I never would've understood why the first solution didn't work.

Now when I face problems in physics or programming, I approach them differently. I ask better questions. I don't see failure as the end—I see it as data. That mindset matters more than the actual fix I made.

I decided freshman year that I wanted to build a solar-powered water filtration system for my community project, mainly because my neighbor Mrs. Chen mentioned her well water tasted metallic and she couldn't afford the $3,000 filter system companies quoted her. I gave myself eight months to design, build, and install it by May.

I broke it down into phases. First three months: research and design. I watched YouTube tutorials, emailed engineers at a local water company, and sketched maybe fifty different configurations. I realized I needed solar panels, a pump, activated charcoal, and sand filters. Second phase was sourcing parts cheaply. I found used solar panels at a recycling center for $200 total and spent weekends rewiring them. My physics teacher Mr. Rodriguez let me test everything in his lab after school.

The actual building phase hit obstacles hard. In February, I miscalculated the water pressure needed and flooded our garage. My dad almost shut the whole thing down. I had to redesign the pump system completely, which cost me three weeks I didn't have. I also discovered mid-March that the charcoal I'd ordered was contaminated, so I spent two weeks finding a legitimate supplier.

By April, I had a working prototype that filtered water down to 99.7% clarity. I installed it at Mrs. Chen's place on May 2nd. She tested it for two weeks before telling me the water actually tasted normal. She cried, which made me cry.

What I learned matters more than the system itself. I learned that deadlines force you to keep moving even when designs fail. I learned asking for help isn't weakness—Mr. Rodriguez and my dad became essential. Most importantly, I learned that real engineering isn't about perfect solutions. It's about building something that actually solves someone's problem, even if it's messy and takes longer than expected.

Last summer, I noticed my neighbor Mrs. Chen couldn't access the city library's online job portal because she didn't have reliable internet. She'd been unemployed for eight months after her factory closed, and I realized the digital divide wasn't just something I'd read about in my civics class—it was happening on Maple Street.

I talked to my friend Derek, who works at the public library in downtown Riverside, and learned that lots of people faced the same barrier. The library had computers, but many older residents felt intimidated by the technology. So Derek and I started a program we called "Tech Bridge" in September. We held free sessions every Tuesday and Thursday evening, teaching basic skills like email, job applications, and resume formatting.

Mrs. Chen came to our first session. She was nervous, but within three weeks she'd created an email account and applied to five positions. She got hired as a customer service representative in October. Watching her confidence grow was incredible.

What surprised me was understanding why the problem existed in the first place. Riverside's internet infrastructure is outdated because the city prioritizes funding for wealthier neighborhoods. The library's computers are outdated because of budget cuts. Mrs. Chen's situation wasn't just about individual effort—it was structural.

By December, we'd worked with fifteen people, and the library committed to making Tech Bridge permanent. They hired Derek part-time to run it.

I learned that prosocial work means looking beyond the immediate problem. It's not enough to help one person; you have to understand why they're struggling and try to change the system. I'm still volunteering there, and I'm now researching public policy programs because I want to work on tech access issues at a larger scale. This experience showed me that engineering solutions matter less without understanding the people and systems they're supposed to serve.

Last summer, I spent six weeks volunteering at the youth center in East Boston where I grew up. I didn't get the grant that first time. But I didn't stop. I reached out to three local tech companies, including one my uncle worked at. By October, we had donations of fifteen refurbished computers and fiber optic equipment. I taught myself how to install everything and spent three weekends doing it with help from two high school friends.

What I learned wasn't just about hardware. Watching those kids actually learn Python and build their first programs—that changed what I want to do. I realized I don't just want to work in tech. I want to solve real infrastructure problems in communities that can't afford solutions.

That's why I'm applying to your engineering program specifically. Your partnership with local governments and emphasis on infrastructure design in underserved areas directly connects to what I started in East Boston. I want to come back and do this work at scale, helping neighborhoods like mine access the resources they deserve.

I spent eight months trying to build a water filtration system for my physics capstone project, and honestly, it was the most frustrating thing I've ever done. My original design in September used activated charcoal and sand layers, but when I tested it in October, the flow rate was impossibly slow. I had to completely rebuild it. But my little sister Emma asked me why I was giving up. She's nine and was working on her own science fair project, and somehow her persistence made me feel stupid for wanting to quit. So I called Mr. Patterson, my physics teacher, and asked if I could come in after school. He showed me how other engineers approach design failures—they document what went wrong and iterate. That changed everything.

I spent January and February testing different materials. I tried PVC alternatives, experimented with varying charcoal ratios, and kept detailed notes on every single test. By March, I finally got a system that filtered one liter in under four minutes with a 94% reduction in turbidity. It wasn't perfect, but it worked.

What I learned wasn't really about water filtration. It was that giving up is easy, and everyone does it sometimes, but pushing past that feeling is what actually matters. I also learned that asking for help isn't weakness—it's smart. Mr. Patterson didn't solve it for me, but he gave me a framework for thinking through problems differently.

Now when I hit obstacles in my engineering classes, I don't panic immediately. I document the failure, adjust my approach, and try again. That eight-month project taught me more about problem-solving than any A grade could have.

My junior year, I decided I wanted to build a website for my neighborhood food bank. Not because anyone asked me to, but because I watched my mom volunteer there and saw how they tracked donations with spreadsheets from 2008. It was chaos.

By November, I had a working prototype. I tested it with three volunteers, including my mom. They found bugs I'd never catch alone—like the donation form not accepting partial amounts. I fixed those, added a simple dashboard showing monthly totals, and launched it December 20th.

What surprised me wasn't completing the project. It was realizing that "I don't know how to code" wasn't actually a barrier—it was just a starting point. I learned that asking for help isn't failure. Marcus didn't write any code for me; he just pointed me toward the solution. Now the food bank processes donations 40% faster.

I'm applying to study computer science because I want to build things that solve actual problems people face, not just theoretical exercises. That project showed me the difference between learning something and using it for something real.

Last spring, our robotics team qualified for the state competition with just eight weeks to build a robot from scratch. He taught me about color correction and how to layer audio properly. It took until early June, way longer than I expected, but I finished it.

When we showed it at the community garden's summer kickoff event, maybe fifty people watched it. Mrs. Chen cried, which I didn't expect. A few people asked if I could make videos for other neighborhood organizations.

I learned that having a goal doesn't mean you actually know how to get there. I was so focused on the finished product that I didn't think about the skills I'd actually need. But I also learned that asking for help isn't giving up. Devon's experience made a real difference, and honestly, I think I want to do more of this kind of work. Last summer, my debate team was falling apart. Last spring, I noticed our school's recycling program was completely broken. Bins were overflowing, contaminated with trash, and most stuff ended up in landfills anyway. I got frustrated watching it fail, so in April I actually did something about it.

The school administration noticed and officially adopted our system in November. Now we've expanded it to all eight lunch periods, and I'm training student volunteers to maintain it.

I learned that leadership isn't about being the loudest person in the room. It's about seeing a problem, doing the research, and building a team with actual expertise. Tyler taught me I didn't need to be an expert myself—I just needed to listen to people who were and communicate their knowledge clearly. I also realized that data matters. Those numbers I tracked convinced people way more than my passion alone ever would have.

Last summer, my neighborhood in East Los Angeles had a water main break that left my street without clean water for three weeks. I'm applying to study civil engineering because I want to come back to LA and work on modernizing our infrastructure. Not as some outside consultant, but as someone who knows these neighborhoods and actually lives here. Your program's partnership with the LA Department of Water and Power is exactly why I'm applying. I want to be the person who finally fixes our system from the inside.

Last summer, I noticed my neighbor Mrs. Chen hadn't picked up her trash cans in three weeks. She's seventy-four and lives alone since her husband passed. I still go over on Thursdays. Her wrist healed, but I keep going because we've become friends. I learned that prosocial stuff isn't some grand gesture you do once. It's small, repeated actions that actually matter to someone real.

Last summer, my dad had a stroke while working at his small auto repair shop in Gary, Indiana. Watching him struggle to remember the names of tools he'd used for thirty years broke something in me. The hospital bills started piling up, and I realized our family wasn't alone—Gary's median household income is $28,000, and most people here can't afford proper healthcare or rehabilitation.

My motivation isn't abstract anymore. It's my dad trying to remember his own phone number. It's Mrs. Chen at the clinic telling me two patients found her because of my app. It's knowing that if I leave and don't come back with skills, nothing changes in Gary. I'm going to college to fix that.

Last summer, I decided to build a weather station for my neighborhood in Portland. What stuck with me is that real projects are messier than school assignments. I learned I need to build in buffer time because things break and fail. I also discovered I actually enjoy problem-solving when it matters for something outside a grade. I'm thinking about environmental engineering now because of this—specifically how to design systems that help communities understand and respond to climate issues.
